questions.stem: A student creates a table comparing xylem and phloem. Which row is correct?

options.text: Xylem: transports sugars, living cells, bidirectional | Phloem: transports water, dead cells, one direction
Xylem: transports water and minerals, dead cells, one direction (up) | Phloem: transports dissolved sugars, living cells, bidirectional
Both transport water and sugars in the same direction using dead cells
Xylem: transports sugars and minerals, living cells | Phloem: transports water only, dead cells

questions.explanation: Xylem transports water and dissolved mineral ions upward from roots to leaves. Xylem vessels are dead cells with lignified walls. Phloem transports dissolved sugars (mainly sucrose) from sources to sinks in both directions. Phloem sieve tubes are living cells supported by companion cells. This is a fundamental comparison in plant biology.

questions.stem: In the human circulatory system, the heart acts as a pump. What is the equivalent 'driving force' for water movement in the xylem of plants?

options.text: Active transport by root cells
Transpiration pull -- evaporation from leaves creates tension that pulls water up through the xylem
Gravity pulling water down through the plant
Osmosis in the leaves pushing water back down

questions.explanation: Plants have no pump equivalent to the heart. Instead, the transpiration stream is driven mainly by evaporation of water from leaf surfaces (transpiration). This creates a tension (negative pressure) that pulls a continuous column of water up through the xylem from the roots. The cohesive properties of water molecules maintain the unbroken column.

questions.stem: Both humans and plants need transport systems because they are multicellular organisms. What is the fundamental reason single-celled organisms do not need specialised transport systems?

options.text: Single-celled organisms do not need nutrients
Single-celled organisms are small enough that diffusion alone can supply all their needs across their entire surface
Single-celled organisms have blood vessels
Single-celled organisms do not respire

questions.explanation: Single-celled organisms have a large surface area to volume ratio. Substances like oxygen and glucose only need to diffuse a very short distance to reach all parts of the cell. In multicellular organisms, many cells are deep inside the body, too far from the external surface for diffusion alone to be efficient, necessitating specialised transport systems.

questions.stem: Blood in human arteries is at high pressure, while sap in phloem moves due to pressure differences between source and sink. However, water in xylem moves under tension (negative pressure). Which statement correctly explains why?

options.text: The heart pushes xylem water just like blood
Xylem water is pulled from above by transpiration (creating tension), whereas blood is pushed from behind by the heart (creating positive pressure)
Xylem water flows downhill by gravity
Negative pressure does not exist in plants

questions.explanation: The key difference is the driving mechanism. Blood is pushed through arteries by the pumping action of the heart (positive pressure). Xylem water is pulled upward by the evaporation of water from leaves, creating a negative pressure (tension) in the xylem. This is the cohesion-tension theory -- water molecules cohere to each other and are pulled upward as a continuous column.

questions.stem: A farmer notices that crops planted too close together grow tall and thin with poor fruit production. Using your knowledge of transport, what might explain the poor fruit development?

options.text: Overcrowded plants produce too much oxygen
Competition for light causes elongated growth; reduced photosynthesis means less sugar is produced and translocated to developing fruits
The plants transport too much water to their fruits
Overcrowded roots cannot carry out mitosis

questions.explanation: When plants are overcrowded, they compete for light, causing them to grow tall and thin (etiolation). With less light per plant, less photosynthesis occurs, meaning less glucose/sucrose is produced. With less sugar available for translocation via phloem, fewer resources reach the developing fruits (sinks), resulting in poor fruit production despite adequate water and minerals.
